analysis.one_liner: Requires gradually lower-carbon transportation fuels for vehicles and aircraft, with labels for low-carbon fuels and land protections.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died there when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to require the EPA to set a declining standard for how much greenhouse gas is emitted per unit of energy in vehicle and aircraft fuels, starting in 2015. Fuel producers would have to cut the carbon intensity of what they sell, earn and trade credits to comply, or pay penalties. It also required labels identifying low-carbon fuels, banned fuels made from biomass harvested from sensitive or newly converted lands, and funded research into lower-carbon jet fuel. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be the public through lower transportation emissions over decades — the bill's stated goal was reductions of 60 to 80 percent by 2050, with transportation fuel responsible for a third of U.S. greenhouse gases. Drivers would get labels identifying which fuels cut emissions at least 20 percent, electric and hydrogen vehicles would be credited for their efficiency, and land and habitat protections would guard against fuel-driven ecosystem conversion. Low-carbon fuel producers, biofuel makers meeting the safeguards, and electric utilities would gain new markets and tradeable credits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public and low-carbon fuel producers

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to set a declining standard cutting greenhouse gases per unit of vehicle-fuel energy by graduated steps — 3 percent in 2015-2019 rising to 21 percent by 2045-2049 — measured against a 2007 baseline.
Requires a low-carbon fuel standard for aircraft fuel, plus a federally funded research program to develop lower-carbon jet fuel alternatives.
Requires the EPA to identify and label low-carbon fuels for consumers by 2009, so drivers can see which fuels cut emissions by at least 20 percent versus the 2007 baseline.

Gives special credit to electricity and hydrogen as vehicle fuels, counting the per-mile efficiency advantage of battery-electric, plug-in hybrid, and hydrogen vehicles — a boost for electric transportation.

Bars transportation fuel derived from biomass taken from ecologically converted lands, sensitive old-growth and roadless areas, conservation reserve and wetland lands, national parks, forests, and refuges, or municipal solid waste — protecting habitats and water quality from fuel-driven land conversion.
Explicitly preserves state authority to address climate change, so state programs like California's would not be overridden.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on producers, importers, and blenders of transportation fuel — chiefly the oil and refining industry — which would have to cut the carbon intensity of their products, buy credits from cleaner fuels, or pay civil penalties of twice the credit market price. Some of that cost would likely have been passed to consumers at the pump; the bill's land-source bans would also restrict some biofuel feedstocks.

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs for refiners, importers, and blenders would likely have been passed to consumers through higher fuel prices, particularly after the standard began tightening in 2020.
The starting standard was modest — only a 3 percent reduction in the first five-year period — so the near-term climate benefit was small even if fully implemented.

The broad bans on fuel from municipal solid waste, recycled paper, and treated wood, and the strict land protections, would have ruled out some feedstocks that biofuel producers consider low-cost, potentially raising the price of compliance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — lower greenhouse gas emissions from transportation, with graduated targets and lifecycle accounting to keep land and air quality from being sacrificed — would have come with real costs: compliance and credit expenses for fuel makers that would partly flow through to consumers as higher prices, and administrative complexity in verifying lifecycle emissions. The design is moderately built: it starts gentle (3 percent) and relies on trading to keep costs down, but its strict sourcing bans could have limited the cheapest low-carbon feedstocks. On balance, an honest weighing favors the bill's climate and fuel-diversity benefits, though its costs on pump prices were real and unquantified. It never got far enough for those trade-offs to be publicly tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House committee and then to a subcommittee the same day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jay Inslee introduced the bill on May 8, 2007 with eight original cosponsors, including Reps. Markey, Pallone, and George Miller.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, which referred it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality — and no further action was ever taken.
It gathered 22 cosponsors, 20 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House, and it was never introduced in the Senate.
When the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, the bill expired; it would have had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil refiners and other transportation fuel producers benefited, since the declining carbon-intensity standard, credit obligations, and civil penalties it would have imposed never took effect.

for.name: Rep. Jay Inslee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered cosponsors; no committee he sat on controlled its fate.

for.name: 20 of 233 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Energy and Commerce members Reps. Markey and Pallone

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearing, no markup, and no vote on the bill in the two years remaining in the Congress.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 20 of 22 cosponsors were Democrats, with 2 Republicans — and the bill's lack of progress came in a committee controlled by the sponsor's own party.

industries.industry: Oil refiners and transportation fuel producers
industries.note: They would have faced a declining cap on the carbon intensity of every gallon sold, with credit purchases and civil penalties for falling short. The bill died before these costs ever took effect.

Low-carbon fuels would earn credits to sell and a government certification label, but the bill bans fuel from municipal solid waste, recycled paper, treated wood, and biomass from newly converted or protected lands, cutting off some feedstocks.
Aircraft fuel would face a standard held at the 2007 baseline with easing only after formal technology and safety reviews, but the bill also funds research into lower-carbon jet fuel alternatives.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and electric vehicle makers
industries.note: The bill credits electricity and hydrogen for the per-mile efficiency of battery-electric, plug-in hybrid, and fuel-cell vehicles, making them more valuable under the standard.
